transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-17
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Torres (AtlasPay CTO), Samir Gupta (AtlasPay Staff ML Eng), Lina Park (AtlasPay SRE)
Artifacts shared: redwood://poc/atlaspay/benchmarks/2026-03-17.csv, deck: https://redwood.app/s/atlaspay-poc, test harness: s3://atlaspay-poc/tests/

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick roll call, um — we have Alex and Priya from Redwood, Maya, Samir, Lina from AtlasPay, all good?
[00:10] Maya Torres: Yep, all good here. Morning for us.
[00:15] Priya Patel: Morning, Maya. Today we're gonna focus on TTFT and streaming, results that we posted to the csv earlier. Alex, do you wanna kick off with the highlights?
[00:25] Alex Chen: Sure, quick TL;DR — this week we ran three main variants: hosted FP16, dedicated int8 quant, and dedicated int8 with warm KV cache + streaming. Primary metric was TTFT (time-to-first-token) and p50/p95 tail for first token and steady state.
[00:40] Samir Gupta: Quick question — when you say "warm KV cache" that's pre-warmed KV on the model server with common prefixes, right?
[00:46] Priya Patel: Correct, we seed the KV with the most common conversation prefixes from your test set so cold-start cost drops. There's some mis- transcription in our notes where it says K-V chache, but it's the cache.
[00:58] [02:10] Alex Chen: Numbers: cold TTFT for the dedicated int8 was around 200-240 ms, FP16 hosted was 150-180 ms for our 256 token prompts. With warm KV + streaming enabled, we got TTFT down to ~95-120 ms on the dedicated cluster. These are median-ish numbers, p95s are higher — around 220-280ms without streaming.
[02:30] Maya Torres: Okay, that's promising. The concern for us is tail latency — our UI can't tolerate p95 over 300ms for initial reply. Did you see any regressions when enabling streaming?
[02:40] Priya Patel: Streaming helped the perceived latency a lot — clients see tokens earlier. However, it introduces a bit of headroom for kernel selection because streaming forces smaller quantization buffers and more frequent kernel launches. We saw a small increase in CPU utilization on the host when we pushed streaming at high concurrency.
[03:05] [05:00] Samir Gupta: Can you remind me which kernels we used? I saw a note about fused attention kernels vs cuBLAS fallback.
[05:08] Priya Patel: Yeah — for the dedicated cluster we tried two kernel sets: the optimized fused-attn kernels (our custom fused kernels tuned for sequence lengths <= 1024) and a more conservative CUTLASS/cuBLAS path which is more stable but slightly slower at short sequence lengths. Fused kernels gave about 10-15% TTFT improvement on average for our test prompts, but were slightly less stable at sequences > 2k — sometimes you get a micro-spike in p95.
[05:35] [07:00] Lina Park: Is that instability reproducible — like a memory fragmentation issue, or is it more deterministic? We need to know for production.
[07:10] Priya Patel: Good question. It's a mix — at extreme sequence lengths the fused path hits different kernel tiling which can expose edge cases under heavy concurrency. We've reproduced it on our perf cluster at 3k seq and concurrency 32. For your workload, where most requests are 256-512 but with a 5% tail at 1k+, it's been fine if we restrict fused kernels to seq <= 1k.
[07:40] [09:00] Alex Chen: Another lever is batching and micro-batching — we tried a continuous batching mode that aggregates tokens across inflight requests. That reduces per-token cost but increases TTFT a bit if you wait for batch fill. For AtlasPay, we found a sweet spot with batch_timeout=10ms and max_batch=8. That kept TTFT in the 100-140ms median while improving throughput about 20%.
[09:25] Samir Gupta: So the tradeoff is cost vs TTFT — do you have numbers about cost delta?
[09:30] Priya Patel: Rough numbers in the CSV: dedicated int8 w/ warm KV + streaming + micro-batching reduced token cost by ~28% vs FP16 hosted at your load profile. We can send that line itemized.
[09:48] [11:00] Maya Torres: The feature gating for streaming — we run streaming only for interactive flows, not for batch, right? How are you suggesting we route?
[11:10] Alex Chen: Exactly. Route by route is the simplest: interactive routes have streaming enabled and strict TTFT SLO, batch routes go through a non-streamed high-throughput pipeline. We can set a policy in the gateway to fall back to smaller model if TTFT penalty exceeds threshold.
[11:30] [13:00] Priya Patel: We also discussed pre-warming strategy — keep a small pool of hot containers per route so cold starts are rare. That costs a bit in reserved capacity but your SLA needs might justify it.
[13:15] Lina Park: For network, we saw some jitter in the test harness when concurrency spiked. Is there a recommended network MTU or keep-alive setting?
[13:25] Priya Patel: Keep-alive of 60s and tuning TCP window to avoid small packetization helps. We'll send recommended host networking settings. Also egress QOS in your pre-prod was throttling at burst — Lina to validate egress policies (action item).
[13:45] [15:00] Alex Chen: Back to kernels: another option is to use hybrid kernel selection — auto-select by sequence length. For seq <= 1k use fused-attn, for >1k fall back to CUTLASS. That got us stable p95 while keeping most of the fused benefit.
[15:20] Samir Gupta: How quickly does the runtime switch? Any warm-up penalty when switching kernel paths mid-stream?
[15:30] Priya Patel: No mid-stream switches — we pick kernel at request start based on estimated final length. There can be an extra micro-config step (~3-5ms) for the kernel launch; it's accounted in TTFT numbers.
[15:50] [17:00] Alex Chen: We also experimented with sequence truncation + progressive decoding: if you expect long continuations, send a short initial prefix to get TTFT low, then stream continuation segments. It reduces initial TTFT but adds complexity to client logic.
[17:20] Maya Torres: That might work for chat flows. Our main concern is regulatory logging and audit trails when splitting requests — will that still be a single logical request?
[17:30] Priya Patel: Yes, we can stitch on the server side and keep request IDs tied. Audit logs will show multiple calls but with same parent request id. We'll note that in the security docs.
[17:50] [19:00] Samir Gupta: About quantization — any quality regressions noticed for int8 vs FP16? We ran an eval suite of 200 prompts, saw a few drop cases on long-context summarization.
[19:10] Priya Patel: Correct, int8 shows tiny score drops in long-form coherence on 3-5% of samples. For AtlasPay's use-case (short replies, templates) it's acceptable, but if you need exact parity for certain routes, we recommend FP16 or selective higher-precision for those routes. Mixed-precision per-route works in Redwood; you can pin model variant at route level.
[19:40] [21:00] Maya Torres: Ok can we get a recommended policy: interactive short -> int8 + fused kernels, interactive long/critical -> FP16, batch -> int8 CU-blas?
[21:10] Alex Chen: That's exactly what we prototyped. We'll include a config template.
[21:20] [23:00] Priya Patel: Quick note on TTFT measurement — our script measures from request send to first token received at the SDK. Make sure your client-side instrumentation isn't masking TLS handshake times. For the benchmarks we disabled TLS overhead by reusing persistent connections; real customer env will have some TLS cost.
[23:20] Lina Park: Good point — TLS reuse is enabled in pre-prod. We'll confirm the client test harness uses persistent HTTP/2 connections.
[23:30] [25:00] Samir Gupta: Anything surprising in the perf logs this week?
[25:10] Priya Patel: One anomaly — on Friday's run we saw a 600ms spike on p99 tied to a GC event in the host runtime when batch size hit 12. We traced it to a rare memory allocation pattern in our request aggregator. We've fixed it in a patch, but we'll push a patch to your pre-prod build so you can validate.
[25:40] Maya Torres: Appreciate that.
[25:50] [27:00] Alex Chen: Next steps recap — we'll share the full CSV and bench harness, Priya will push kernel traces and the patch, you (Maya/Samir/Lina) will run the pre-prod streaming test at 1k seq and report back. Also schedule the canary for the week after.
[27:30] Maya Torres: Sounds good. One more: can you include cost delta estimates in the CSV per 10k requests? Finance wants a simple line-item.
[27:40] Alex Chen: Yep we'll add a cost-per-10k-requests line and assumptions (tokens per request, concurrency).
[27:50] [29:00] Priya Patel: I'll also include a kernel recommendation table: seq buckets and recommended kernels/precision and a short note on stability.
[29:10] Samir Gupta: For action items, Samir will validate the test harness and share logs if anything funky.
[29:20] Alex Chen: Great. Any blocker to running the pre-prod tests this week?
[29:30] Lina Park: No blockers, just need the patched image and the bench script, which you said you'd share.
[29:40] Alex Chen: We'll drop everything in the s3 test path by EOD tomorrow.
[29:50] [31:00] Maya Torres: Ok, thanks all.
[31:05] Priya Patel: Quick note — we noticed a tiny regression when enabling request-level encryption with your KMS. There's a 5-7ms overhead on the crypto ops; nothing huge but called it out because it adds up on p95.
[31:20] Maya Torres: Noted, we'll weigh that versus compliance needs.
[31:30] [33:00] Alex Chen: Final recap of next steps and owners: Alex - share CSV & cost lines, Priya - kernel traces + patch, Lina - verify egress/QoS, Maya/Samir - run streaming pre-prod 1k seq and report. Can we reconvene next Tuesday same time?
[33:20] Maya Torres: Yes, next Tuesday 14:00 UTC works.
[33:30] Samir Gupta: Thanks everyone, appreciate the detailed notes.
[33:40] Alex Chen: Thanks team — we'll follow up in writing with the artifacts and action item list.
[34:00] Meeting end.
